source.title: LightSAM: Parameter-Agnostic Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Yi-Fei Cheng; Li Shen; Hao Sun; Nan Yin; Xiao-Chun Cao; Enhong Chen

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure text and a table in the PDF extraction are garbled or flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares sharpness-aware methods and reports that the proposed adaptive optimizer improves held-out performance in its tested tasks; it does not measure sharpness or the training–test gap as V7 specifies, so this is a refinement of the optimizer/generalization discussion rather than a direct V7 test. Its reported optimizer comparisons also bear on V4 in a distinct setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark test accuracies and training-loss curves for optimizer comparisons, but does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, architecture/local connectivity, dropout, generalization-gap measures, or removal of memorized examples. Hyperparameter values are not rows; they define experimental settings. Figure 1's curves are described qualitatively in the text, with no recoverable numeric values.
record.test_reason: The plain Adam/AdaGrad versus SGD benchmark comparisons bear on V4, including new transformer fine-tuning settings. These comparisons use selected learning rates rather than a documented, matched tuning search, so conclusions apply to the reported recipes. SAM performance does not test V7's sharpness–generalization-gap correlation.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase captures the authors' conclusion: LightSAM adapts perturbation and update steps, achieves the stated convergence rate under assumptions, and shows competitive performance and reduced hyperparameter sensitivity in preliminary experiments. However, unrestricted parameter choices are established in Theorems 1–2 for the AdaGrad variants; Theorem 3 for the Adam variant imposes momentum constraints and horizon-dependent learning-rate and perturbation-radius scaling. The authors' blanket parameter-agnostic conclusion overstates that theorem.
record.recipe_differences: Proposes adaptive SAM variants using AdaGrad-Norm, AdaGrad, or Adam for perturbation and model updates; experiments compare optimizer test metrics on MNIST, ImageNet fine-tuning, and GLUE fine-tuning. The original claim concerns natural-label generalization and training–test gaps, which this paper does not measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported optimizer outcomes vary by dataset/task and model; on GLUE, LightSAM is highest on seven tasks but not QNLI. Tables V and VII report sensitivity to learning rate and perturbation radius; SAM and ASAM fail to converge in some tested settings, while LightSAM has lower variability in the reported averages.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding SAM-family perturbations generally improves benchmark performance over the corresponding base optimizer; LightSAM also shows relatively low variability across tested hyperparameter settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive perturbation and update rules can improve benchmark performance and reduce sensitivity to learning rate and perturbation radius in the tested recipes.

record.problems: No training error or train–test gap is reported for the benchmark comparisons. Experiments use selected hyperparameters and report best test scores; MNIST sensitivity results are averages across four settings and tables report standard deviations, while the paper calls its experiments preliminary. The GLUE section says eight tasks, but the supplied Table VI displays seven named task columns plus an average.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted. Figure 1 contains training-loss and test-accuracy curves, but the supplied extraction is garbled and no numeric values can be recovered; the paper describes them qualitatively in the Results on ImageNet text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
A documented convolutional-versus-fully-connected architectural comparison and the contribution of local connectivity. The three-layer model's connectivity is not specified in the supplied text.

Matched learning-rate and decay tuning searches; broader tuning of plain optimizers; decoupled weight decay; switching from Adam to SGD; word-level language modeling. The equal-or-better-training-performance clause is not established for the plain optimizer comparisons.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and remedies for large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions, small-data dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with training–test gaps, and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Missing training–test gaps do not disqualify the direct held-out optimizer comparisons from V4. Conversely, better SAM benchmark performance alone does not establish V7. The record incorrectly says no training loss is reported: Figure 1 and its discussion report ViT training-loss trajectories, already declared in rows_left_out. It also incorrectly describes Table VI as having only seven task columns; the supplied text contains eight. The conditional V4 challenges do not establish that adaptive methods generally outperform tuned SGD.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond zero training error.
The paper compares SAM-family optimizers and base optimizers, not the adaptive-versus-SGD claim under matched limited tuning; broader tuning and the cited language-model exception are not tested.
Large-batch versus small-batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its association with the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining.
